l: Abimelech, The Book of Judges
s: Abimelech is a son of Gideon (Jerubbaal) by a female servant. Backed by Shechem, he hires reckless men with silver from Baal Berith's house, kills his seventy brothers, and is made king. After three years Shechem betrays him; he destroys it, then attacks Thebez, where a woman's millstone fatally wounds him and he has his armor bearer finish him.

l: house of Jerubbaal, The Book of Judges
s: has_count seventy The seventy sons of Jerubbaal are killed by Abimelech on one stone at Ophrah. Only the youngest, Jotham, survives. Their blood is said to be laid on Abimelech and the men of Shechem.

l: battle with Midian, The Book of Judges
s: has_outcome Midian subdued [land rested forty years] The Ephraimites complain they were not called to the fight, and Gideon soothes them by citing their capture of Oreb and Zeeb. Gideon's three hundred men pursue and strike the Midianite army of about fifteen thousand at Karkor, confuse it, and capture Zebah and Zalmunna. The victory leaves Midian subdued and the land at rest for forty years.

l: Jotham, The Book of Judges
s: Jotham, Jerubbaal's youngest son, survives a massacre by hiding, then tells the parable of the trees from Mount Gerizim, curses Abimelech and Shechem with fire, and flees to Beer; his curse ultimately comes true.

l: men of Shechem, The Book of Judges
s: The men of Shechem back Abimelech as brother, fund his killers and crown him; after God sends an evil spirit they betray him, trust Gaal, and Abimelech kills them, about a thousand burning.

l: parable of the trees, The Book of Judges
s: Jotham's parable in Chapter 9: olive, fig, and vine refuse kingship over the trees to keep oil, fruit, and wine; the bramble accepts, threatening fire against the cedars; Jotham applies it to Abimelech and Shechem.

l: Gaal, The Book of Judges
s: Gaal, son of Ebed, arrives in Shechem with his brothers, gains the men's trust, incites them against Abimelech, but is taunted by Zebul, loses the fight, and is driven out.

l: Zebul, The Book of Judges
s: Zebul is Shechem's ruler and Abimelech's officer; angered by Gaal's words, he secretly warns Abimelech to ambush, taunts Gaal into fighting, then drives Gaal and his brothers out.

l: Thebez, The Book of Judges
s: has_part tower of Thebez [strong tower within the city] Abimelech camps against Thebez and takes it. The people flee into a strong tower within the city, and during his attack on its door a woman's millstone kills him.

l: woman of Thebez, The Book of Judges
s: killed Abimelech [with an upper millstone] A certain woman on the tower roof at Thebez casts an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and breaks his skull. This leads to his death.

l: destruction of Shechem, The Book of Judges
s: is_a city destroyed and sown with salt by Abimelech Abimelech divides his people into companies, strikes those coming out of the city, fights all day, takes the city, kills its people, beats it down, and sows it with salt. He then burns the stronghold of the house of Elberith over the men of the tower, killing about a thousand men and women.

l: Jotham's curse, The Book of Judges
s: fell_on men of Shechem [fulfilled by God] Jotham prays that fire come out from Abimelech to devour Shechem and from Shechem to devour Abimelech if they have not dealt rightly with Jerubbaal's house. The chapter ends by saying the curse came on the men of Shechem, as Abimelech and Shechem destroy each other.

l: Jair, The Book of Judges
s: Jair, a Gileadite, judged Israel twenty-two years after Tola. His thirty sons rode donkey colts and held thirty cities called Havvoth Jair in Gilead; he died and was buried in Kamon.

l: Gilead, The Book of Judges
s: Gilead is the land of Jair's thirty cities, called Havvoth Jair. It was where the Amorites lived and where Israelites beyond the Jordan were oppressed for eighteen years. The Ammonites encamped there, and its princes offered headship over all Gilead's inhabitants to whoever would begin the fight against them.

l: Israel's sin and idolatry (Israel), The Book of Judges
s: Israel again did evil, serving the Baals, the Ashtaroth and the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, Ammon and the Philistines, and abandoned the LORD. They confessed having forsaken God, and the LORD said he would save them no more and told them to cry to their chosen gods. Israel then admitted its sin, asked for deliverance, and put away the foreign gods to serve the LORD.

l: Ammonite oppression (Israel), The Book of Judges
s: A war waged by the Ammonites against Israel. Because of the LORD's anger, Israel was sold to the Philistines and Ammonites, who oppressed them eighteen years, especially in Gilead, and crossed the Jordan against Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim. Israel cried out. Ammon then claimed land from the Arnon to the Jabbok; after failed diplomacy, Jephthah advanced and the LORD delivered Ammon to him, subjugating it.

l: Jephthah the Gileadite, The Book of Judges
s: Jephthah the Gileadite is a mighty man of valor, son of Gilead and a prostitute. Driven out by his half-brothers, he lives in Tob with outlaws until the elders recall him as head and chief of Gilead. He argues Israel's case to the Ammonite king, vows to the LORD, defeats Ammon, and carries out the vow when his only daughter meets him. He then fights Ephraim, judges Israel six years, and is buried in Gilead's cities.

l: elders of Gilead, The Book of Judges
s: The elders of Gilead, who had earlier hated Jephthah and driven him out, go to Tob to fetch him when Ammon makes war. They promise him headship over all the inhabitants of Gilead, call the LORD witness between them, and the people make him head and chief.

l: king of the children of Ammon, The Book of Judges
s: The king claims that Israel took Ammon's land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and the Jordan when it came out of Egypt, and demands its peaceable return. Jephthah replies twice with historical arguments, but the king does not listen to his words.

l: Jephthah's vow, The Book of Judges
s: promises burnt offering of whatever first comes out of his house [to the LORD, if he delivers Ammon] Jephthah vows that if the LORD delivers Ammon into his hand, whatever comes out of his house doors to meet him on his peaceful return will be the LORD's and he will offer it as a burnt offering. The LORD grants the victory, his daughter is the first to come out, and Jephthah says he cannot go back on what he has said to the LORD; he does with her according to the vow.

l: Jephthah's daughter, The Book of Judges
s: Jephthah the Gileadite's only child, a virgin, greets him with tambourines and dances after his victory, accepts his vow, mourns her virginity two months with companions, returns, and is fulfilled by him; Israel's daughters commemorate her yearly four days.

l: Shibboleth, The Book of Judges
s: is_a password word [test used to identify Ephraimites by pronunciation] 'Shibboleth' is the word the Gileadites make suspected Ephraimites say at the Jordan fords. Those who say 'Sibboleth' because they cannot pronounce it correctly are seized and killed.

l: Ibzan, The Book of Judges
s: Ibzan of Bethlehem succeeds Jephthah as judge of Israel, fathers thirty sons and thirty daughters whom he marries outside and inside his clan, judges seven years, then dies and is buried in Bethlehem.

l: Elon, The Book of Judges
s: Elon, a Zebulunite, judges Israel for ten years after Ibzan, then dies and is buried in Aijalon in Zebulun's land.

l: Abdon, The Book of Judges
s: Abdon, son of Hillel the Pirathonite, judges Israel for eight years after Elon, has forty sons and thirty grandsons riding seventy donkey colts, then dies and is buried in Pirathon in Ephraim.

l: battle between Gilead and Ephraim, The Book of Judges
s: Threatened by Ephraim, Jephthah's Gilead men defeat them, seize the Jordan fords, and kill fugitives failing the 'Shibboleth' test; forty-two thousand Ephraimites die.

l: Manoah, The Book of Judges
s: Manoah is a Danite man of Zorah who prays for guidance in raising a promised child, questions an angel, offers a young goat and burnt offering, then fears death after realizing the angel's identity, but his wife reassures him.

l: wife of Manoah, The Book of Judges
s: Manoah's wife, initially barren and childless, is told by the LORD's angel she will bear a son and must avoid wine, strong drink, and unclean food. She reports it to her husband, fetches him, calms his fear of death with reasoning, and then bears Samson.

l: angel of the LORD (messenger to Manoah and his wife), The Book of Judges
s: A messenger sent by the LORD who appears to Manoah's wife announcing a Nazirite son to begin saving Israel from the Philistines, returns to instruct Manoah, refuses food and his incomprehensible name, directs a burnt offering, then ascends in the altar flame, revealing his identity.

l: Samson, The Book of Judges
s: Samson is the son of Manoah and his wife, promised before conception as a Nazirite to God from the womb, bound by a vow forbidding a razor on his head, and destined to begin saving Israel from the Philistines. Blessed by the LORD and moved by the LORD's Spirit, he is marked by great strength and quick anger. He sees a Philistine woman in Timnah and insists on marrying her, kills a lion bare-handed, and poses a riddle at his wedding feast to thirty companions. When his wife betrays the answer, he kills thirty men at Ashkelon, returns angrily to his father's house, and loses her to his companion. Refused entry when he later visits her, he burns the Philistines' crops with foxes and strikes them hip and thigh. Bound by the men of Judah, he breaks free and kills a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone, then is revived by water God provides. He judges Israel twenty years. In Gaza he carries off the city gate, then loves Delilah. After deceiving her three times, he reveals the secret of his hair, is shaved, blinded, bound in bronze fetters and made to grind at the prison mill. He prays to the LORD, brings down the house of Dagon on himself and the Philistines, and is buried in his father's burial site between Zorah and Eshtaol.

l: Danites, The Book of Judges
s: The Danites are a tribe of Israel descended from Dan, who had not yet received an inheritance among the tribes. They sent five valiant men to spy out land, then marched with six hundred armed men, seizing Micah's idols, ephod, and priest. They conquered and burned Laish, rebuilt it as Dan, and installed the image, with Jonathan and his sons as priests.

l: Nazirite vow, The Book of Judges
s: The Nazirite vow is a consecration to God from the womb to death, forbidding a razor on the head. An angel announces it for the promised child, with his mother avoiding wine, strong drink, uncleanness and vine products. Later Samson reveals he has kept it, and says shaving would remove his strength.

l: burnt offering (Manoah's offering), The Book of Judges
s: is_offered_to LORD [by Manoah, young goat with meal offering] At the angel's direction, Manoah offered a young goat with a meal offering on the rock to the LORD. As the flame rose from the altar, the angel ascended in it while Manoah and his wife watched and fell on their faces. Manoah's wife later cited the LORD's acceptance of this offering as evidence that he did not intend to kill them.

l: Samson's wife, The Book of Judges
s: A Philistine woman from Timnah whom Samson asks his parents to get as his wife. Threatened with burning by the thirty companions, she weeps seven days, learns the riddle from Samson and tells her people, then is given to his friend.

l: Timnah, The Book of Judges
s: Timnah is where Samson sees and later talks with the Philistine woman he wants as wife. Its vineyards are where the young lion roars at him, and it is the place of the marriage feast.

l: young lion (Samson's kill), The Book of Judges
s: located_in vineyards of Timnah [roared at Samson there] A young lion roars at Samson in the vineyards of Timnah, and he tears it apart with his bare hands as if it were a young goat, by the LORD's Spirit. Its carcass later holds a swarm of bees and honey, which become the basis of his riddle.

l: bees and honey (in the lion's carcass), The Book of Judges
s: located_in young lion (Samson's kill) [in the carcass] Samson finds a swarm of bees and honey in the lion's carcass. He eats the honey as he goes and gives some to his parents without telling them where it came from. This secret is the hidden answer to his riddle.

l: wedding feast (Samson's feast), The Book of Judges
s: lasts seven days Samson holds a feast in Timnah, as young men used to do, and thirty companions are brought to be with him. It lasts seven days, during which he poses his riddle and his wife weeps to learn its answer.

l: thirty companions (at Samson's feast), The Book of Judges
s: attends wedding feast (Samson's feast) [brought to be with Samson] Thirty companions are brought to be with Samson at his feast. They cannot solve his riddle in three days, so on the seventh day they threaten Samson's wife with burning to make her get the answer. They then answer the riddle before sunset and receive the garments Samson pays from the plunder at Ashkelon.

l: riddle (Samson's riddle), The Book of Judges
s: has_answer honey from the lion ["What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?"] Samson's riddle is: "Out of the eater came out food. Out of the strong came out sweetness." The companions fail for three days, then learn the answer through his wife and reply, "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" Samson says they have plowed with his heifer.

l: wager garments (thirty linen garments and changes of clothing), The Book of Judges
s: is_stake_of riddle (Samson's riddle) [owed by the losing side] Samson stakes thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing on the riddle, with the same owed to him if the companions fail. When they answer correctly, he pays the changes of clothing to them, taking them as plunder from the thirty men he strikes at Ashkelon.

l: thirty men of Ashkelon, The Book of Judges
s: located_in Ashkelon [struck by Samson] Thirty men of Ashkelon are struck by Samson. He takes their plunder and uses the changes of clothing to pay those who declared his riddle.

l: Samson's wife, The Book of Judges
s: Samson's wife, daughter of a father and elder sister of a more beautiful younger sister, is given by her father to Samson's companion, barring Samson from her; the Philistines then burn her to death over Samson's crop burning.

l: father of Samson's wife, The Book of Judges
s: He refuses to let Samson into his daughter's room, saying he thought Samson utterly hated her and so gave her to Samson's companion. He offers Samson her younger sister instead, and is later burned with fire by the Philistines along with his daughter.

l: men of Judah, The Book of Judges
s: are_ruled_by Philistines Three thousand men of Judah go down to the cave in Etam's rock to bind Samson and deliver him to the Philistines, reminding him that the Philistines rule over them. They get his agreement not to be attacked by them, bind him with two new ropes, promise not to kill him, and bring him up from the rock to Lehi.

l: foxes (Samson's three hundred foxes), The Book of Judges
s: has_quantity three hundred Samson catches three hundred foxes, turns them tail to tail, and puts a torch between every two tails. Once the torches are lit, he lets the foxes go into the Philistines' standing grain.

l: Philistine crops (standing grain, shocks, olive groves), The Book of Judges
s: The standing grain, the shocks, and the olive groves of the Philistines are set ablaze by the torch-carrying foxes and burned up.

l: burning of the Philistine crops, The Book of Judges
s: Samson does this in retaliation after his wife is given to his companion, saying he will be blameless in the case of the Philistines when he harms them. It prompts the Philistines to ask who did it and to burn Samson's wife and her father in response.

l: cave in Etam's rock, The Book of Judges
s: located_in Judah [men of Judah went down to it] After striking the Philistines with great slaughter, Samson goes down and lives in the cave in Etam's rock. The men of Judah come to it to bind him, and he is brought up from the rock bound with two new ropes.

l: Lehi, The Book of Judges
s: The Philistines spread themselves in Lehi after encamping in Judah. Samson is brought there bound, breaks free, and strikes a thousand men with a jawbone. The place where he throws the jawbone is called Ramath Lehi, and God splits the hollow place in Lehi to give him water.

l: jawbone of a donkey, The Book of Judges
s: has_state fresh Samson finds a fresh donkey's jawbone, takes it, and strikes a thousand men with it, then composes a verse about it. He throws it out of his hand when he finishes speaking, and the place is called Ramath Lehi.

l: Samson's slaughter of a thousand men, The Book of Judges
s: uses jawbone of a donkey [weapon] At Lehi, after breaking his bonds, Samson strikes a thousand men with a fresh donkey's jawbone. He commemorates it saying, 'heaps on heaps; with the jawbone of a donkey I have struck a thousand men.'

l: En Hakkore, The Book of Judges
s: located_in Lehi [water from split hollow place] En Hakkore is the name given to the spring of water that comes out of the hollow place God splits in Lehi after Samson prays. The text says it bears this name to this day.

l: Delilah, The Book of Judges
s: lives_in valley of Sorek Delilah, a woman Samson loves in the valley of Sorek, is offered eleven hundred pieces of silver by each of the lords of the Philistines to discover the source of his strength. She tests three false answers on him, presses him daily until he tells all, then calls the lords, has his seven locks shaved while he sleeps on her knees, and begins to afflict him.

l: lords of the Philistines, The Book of Judges
s: rule Philistines The lords of the Philistines come up to Delilah and promise each to give her eleven hundred pieces of silver if she learns Samson's secret. They bring seven green cords, then come again with the money after she says he has told all. They gather to sacrifice to Dagon and are present in the house when it falls on them.

l: Samson's hair, The Book of Judges
s: Samson's seven locks survive a false loom test, but Delilah has them shaved while he sleeps, costing his strength; afterward the hair begins growing again.

l: Samson's strength, The Book of Judges
s: depends_on Samson's hair [lost if shaved] Samson's strength lets him carry the Gaza gate doors with the posts to a mountain before Hebron and break green cords, new ropes and a loom pin. It leaves him when his locks are shaved, and he does not know the LORD has departed. He asks the LORD to strengthen him this once, and with it he bows the pillars.

l: house of Dagon, The Book of Judges
s: is_supported_by pillars (of the house) [two middle pillars] The house is where the Philistine lords gather to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god, rejoicing that he has delivered Samson. It is full of men and women, with about three thousand more on the roof watching Samson perform. It falls on the lords and all the people in it.

l: pillars (of the house), The Book of Judges
s: Samson is set between the pillars and asks the boy holding his hand to let him feel the pillars on which the house rests so he can lean on them. He takes hold of the two middle pillars, one with each hand, and bows with all his might.

l: Samson's death and the collapse of the house, The Book of Judges
s: killed more people than Samson's life [the dead killed at his death exceeded those killed in his life] Samson says, "Let me die with the Philistines!" and bows himself, and the house falls on the lords and all the people in it. The dead he kills at his death outnumber those he killed in his life. His brothers and his father's house bring him up and bury him between Zorah and Eshtaol in Manoah's burial site.

l: Micah, The Book of Judges
s: Micah is a man of the hill country of Ephraim. He confesses to his mother that he took her eleven hundred pieces of silver and returns it. He then keeps a house of gods holding a carved image, a molten image, an ephod, and teraphim. He first consecrates one of his sons as priest, then hires a wandering young Levite, believing the LORD will do him good. Later the Danites take the images and the priest. Micah protests that he is left with nothing, but they warn him of angry men and he sees their strength, so he goes home.

l: Micah's mother, The Book of Judges
s: Micah's mother loses eleven hundred silver pieces and curses; when her son returns them, she blesses him, dedicates the silver to the LORD for carved and molten images, and pays a silversmith two hundred pieces.

l: eleven hundred pieces of silver, The Book of Judges
s: owner Micah's mother [taken from her, then restored] The eleven hundred pieces of silver were taken from Micah's mother, who cursed the theft, and Micah admits he took them. He restores them, and his mother dedicates them to the LORD for making images. Two hundred pieces are given to a silversmith to make the carved image and molten image.

l: carved image and molten image (Micah's), The Book of Judges
s: Micah's carved and molten images were made by a silversmith from two hundred pieces of silver and placed in Micah's house of gods with an ephod and teraphim. Five men identified them, and the Danites took them from Micah's house while the priest stood at the gate. They carried them to Laish, setting up the engraved image, which remained while God's house was in Shiloh.

l: Levite (young man of Bethlehem Judah), The Book of Judges
s: A young Levite from Bethlehem Judah who leaves his city seeking a place to live and reaches Micah's house in Ephraim. Micah hires him as father and priest for silver, clothing, and food, and consecrates him. When five Danite men recognize him, he tells them their way is before the LORD. Invited to be priest to a whole tribe, he gladly takes the ephod, teraphim, and image and goes with them. He is identified as Jonathan, son of Gershom, son of Moses, serving the Danites until the captivity.

l: Bethlehem Judah, The Book of Judges
s: Bethlehem Judah is where the Levite takes his concubine from and where her father's house is, to which she returns for four months. The Levite stays there several days before leaving for the hill country of Ephraim.

l: priesthood arrangement (Micah and the Levite), The Book of Judges
s: Micah offers the Levite a position as father and priest in exchange for ten pieces of silver per year, a suit of clothing, and his food, and the Levite accepts. Micah consecrates him, replacing the earlier arrangement in which one of his sons was priest. Micah then says he knows the LORD will do him good because he has a Levite as priest.

l: five men, The Book of Judges
s: Five valiant Danite men from Zorah and Eshtaol are sent to spy out the land, lodge at Micah's house and consult the Levite, see Laish living safely, urge attack, then on return help take the ephod and images.

l: Laish, The Book of Judges
s: Laish was a quiet, secure valley city near Beth Rehob, far from Sidon, with no deliverer or ruler; the Danites struck it with the sword, burned it, rebuilt it, and renamed it Dan after their father.

l: people of Laish, The Book of Judges
s: The people of Laish were a quiet, secure, isolated people living like the Sidonians, with no allies or authority in the land. Spies found them unsuspecting; the Danites struck them with the sword, and no one rescued them because Sidon was far.

l: Shiloh, The Book of Judges
s: Shiloh is a place in Canaan, north of Bethel and south of Lebonah, east of the Bethel–Shechem highway; it hosts the yearly feast of the LORD and receives the 400 virgins brought to the camp.

l: Levite (the concubine's husband), The Book of Judges
s: The Levite is the husband of a concubine. He travels to Bethlehem Judah to win her back, stays with her father, then leaves and lodges in Gibeah, where he gives her to the city's men. Finding her fallen at the door, he takes her home, cuts her into twelve pieces, and sends them through Israel. At Mizpah he recounts the attack to the assembly and asks their counsel.

l: concubine (the Levite's concubine), The Book of Judges
s: The Levite's concubine left him for her father's house in Bethlehem Judah, staying four months until he came for her. At Gibeah she was thrown to a mob, raped and abused all night, and died at the door. The Levite cut her body into twelve pieces and sent them through Israel, prompting the tribes to gather.

l: father-in-law (the concubine's father), The Book of Judges
s: The young woman's father rejoices to see the Levite and keeps him in his house, urging him with food, drink, and merriment to stay through several days. His repeated urging delays the Levite's departure until the day is nearly over on the fifth day.

l: old man (of Gibeah), The Book of Judges
s: An old man from the hill country of Ephraim, living in Gibeah, sees the travelers in the street, offers to supply all their needs, and takes them into his house. When the men of the city demand the Levite, he pleads with them not to act wickedly and offers his virgin daughter and the Levite's concubine instead.

l: men of Gibeah (wicked fellows), The Book of Judges
s: Wicked men of the city surround the old man's house, beat at the door, and demand that the Levite be brought out so they can have sex with him. They refuse the old man's plea, take the concubine, rape and abuse her all night, and let her go at dawn. According to the Levite, the men of Gibeah surrounded the house by night, intended to kill him and raped his concubine until she was dead. Israel demands that the wicked men among them be delivered up for death, and Gibeah contributes seven hundred chosen men to Benjamin's army before the city is destroyed.

l: Gibeah, The Book of Judges
s: Gibeah is a Benjamite city whose inhabitants refuse the Levite's party shelter until an Ephraimite old man takes them in, and whose men assault the concubine. Israel assembles against it; its seven hundred chosen men fight alongside Benjamin, but ambushers rush the city, strike it with the sword, and burn it entirely.

l: gang rape and abuse of the concubine, The Book of Judges
s: In Gibeah, men of Gibeah rape and abuse the Levite's concubine all night after he sends her out to the mob; at dawn she collapses at the door, unresponsive.

l: dismemberment of the concubine, The Book of Judges
s: At home, a Levite cuts his concubine limb by limb into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel's borders; viewers call it unprecedented since leaving Egypt and demand consideration and counsel.

l: ambushers, The Book of Judges
s: Israel sets ambushers around Gibeah, and they break out of their place when Israel's main force feigns flight at Baal Tamar. They rush Gibeah, strike the city with the sword and raise the great cloud of smoke as the appointed sign, which turns the battle against Benjamin.

l: battle between Israel and Benjamin, The Book of Judges
s: has_outcome 25,000 Benjamite swordsmen fell [third day] Benjamin wins the first two days, killing twenty-two thousand and then eighteen thousand Israelites, using its seven hundred left-handed slingers among others. On the third day Israel draws Benjamin from the city, the ambushers burn Gibeah, and Benjamin's army is routed, with twenty-five thousand swordsmen dead and six hundred fleeing to the rock of Rimmon, where they stay four months.

l: outrage at Gibeah, The Book of Judges
s: is_described_as wickedness [lewdness and folly in Israel] The outrage is the attack on the Levite and the rape and death of his concubine, called wickedness, lewdness and folly in Israel. It is the cause of Israel's assembly, its demand that the guilty men be put to death to put away evil from Israel, and the war that follows when Benjamin refuses.

l: Jabesh Gilead, The Book of Judges
s: Jabesh Gilead is a place that alone sent no one to the Mizpah assembly; the congregation's army then struck its inhabitants with the sword, sparing only four hundred young virgins.

l: four hundred young virgins of Jabesh Gilead, The Book of Judges
s: Four hundred virgins who had not lain with a man are found in Jabesh Gilead, brought to Shiloh's camp, and given to Benjamin, but they fall short of the men's needs.

l: daughters of Shiloh, The Book of Judges
s: practice dancing at the feast [come out to dance in the dances] The daughters of Shiloh come out to dance at the feast. The Benjamites, hiding in the vineyards, each catch one of them as a wife and carry them off to the land of Benjamin.

l: oath at Mizpah, The Book of Judges
s: Israel's men swore at Mizpah, under a curse, not to give daughters to Benjamin as wives, and also swore death for anyone not coming up to the LORD there. These oaths create the problem of finding Benjamin wives, driving actions against Jabesh Gilead and Shiloh.

l: feast of the LORD, The Book of Judges
s: occurs yearly [at Shiloh] The feast of the LORD is held from year to year in Shiloh. The elders choose it as the time when the Benjamites may take wives from the dancing daughters of Shiloh.

l: abduction of the daughters of Shiloh, The Book of Judges
s: is_carried_out_by Benjamin [to obtain wives] On the elders' instruction, the Benjamites lie in wait in the vineyards and each catch a wife from the dancing daughters of Shiloh. The elders plan to tell complaining fathers and brothers that the men took them neither in battle nor by being given, so Israel would not be guilty by giving.

l: slaughter of Jabesh Gilead, The Book of Judges
s: The congregation sends twelve thousand valiant men to strike Jabesh Gilead with the sword, destroying every male and every woman who has lain with a man, while sparing four hundred young virgins.

l: The First Book of Samuel
s: This is the book of 1 Samuel, a narrative of Israel's transition from judges to monarchy, centered on Samuel, Saul, and David, with the LORD's guidance and judgment as the driving force. It opens with Hannah, barren and provoked by Peninnah, vowing a son to the LORD; Samuel is born and given to Eli at Shiloh. Eli's wicked sons Hophni and Phinehas are condemned, and the young Samuel is called as prophet. Israel loses the ark to the Philistines in battle, Hophni, Phinehas and Eli die, and the ark afflicts Dagon and Philistine cities until it is returned and rests at Kiriath Jearim. Samuel leads Israel back to the LORD and judges them, but when his sons take bribes the elders demand a king. Despite warnings that this rejects the LORD as king, Samuel anoints Saul, a tall Benjamite looking for lost donkeys. Saul is chosen at Mizpah, rescues Jabesh Gilead from Nahash, and is confirmed at Gilgal; Samuel gives a farewell address. Saul's reign then falters: he offers the sacrifice himself rather than waiting for Samuel, and spares Agag and the best livestock of Amalek, so Samuel declares that obedience is better than sacrifice and that the kingdom is torn from him. Meanwhile Jonathan's bold attacks defeat Philistines. The LORD sends Samuel to anoint David, Jesse's youngest son, whose harp soothes Saul, and who kills Goliath with a sling. Saul's jealousy grows after the women's song, and he repeatedly tries to kill David. Jonathan covenants with David and protects him, and Michal helps him escape. David flees, receives bread and Goliath's sword at Nob, and gathers a band of about four hundred, later six hundred. Saul has Doeg kill eighty-five priests of Nob; Abiathar escapes to David. David saves Keilah, is pursued through wilderness, and twice spares Saul, the LORD's anointed, in a cave at En Gedi and in Saul's camp, while Saul admits his guilt. Samuel dies, and Abigail restrains David from vengeance on Nabal, then becomes his wife after Nabal dies. David takes refuge with Achish of Gath at Ziklag but is sent back by the Philistine princes before the final battle. He recovers his family and goods from the Amalekites and shares the plunder fairly. Saul, abandoned by the LORD, consults the woman of Endor, and Samuel's spirit foretells his death. The book ends on Mount Gilboa, where Saul and his sons, including Jonathan, die. The Philistines display Saul's body, and the men of Jabesh Gilead retrieve and bury it.

l: Elkanah, The First Book of Samuel
s: Elkanah is an Ephraimite, son of Jeroham, living at Ramathaim Zophim with two wives, Hannah and Peninnah. He yearly worships and sacrifices at Shiloh, favoring beloved Hannah with a double portion. He fathers Samuel, and after Samuel is weaned he goes up with his household to offer sacrifice and his vow.

l: Hannah, The First Book of Samuel
s: Hannah is Elkanah's beloved wife, childless and severely provoked each year by her rival Peninnah. At Shiloh she weeps, prays in bitterness, and vows to give a son to the LORD. After Eli blesses her, she bears Samuel, weans him, and brings him to Eli to fulfill the vow. She sings a prayer of rejoicing, makes Samuel a robe yearly, and the LORD later gives her three more sons and two daughters.

l: Peninnah, The First Book of Samuel
s: Peninnah is Elkanah's other wife, mother of sons and daughters who received portions at sacrifice; as Hannah's rival, she provoked and irritated Hannah severely year after year at the LORD's house.

l: Eli, The First Book of Samuel
s: Eli is an elderly priest of the LORD at the temple in Shiloh who judged Israel for forty years and fathered Hophni and Phinehas. He first appears misreading Hannah's silent prayer as drunkenness, then blesses her and asks God to grant her petition; she later brings the child Samuel to him. Very old, Eli hears of his sons' misdeeds and rebukes them, but they do not listen. A man of God announces that his house will be cut off and both sons will die in one day. With his eyesight dim, Eli realizes the LORD is calling Samuel and instructs him how to answer. He accepts the judgment Samuel reports, saying it is the LORD's will. At ninety-eight and blind, he waits by the road, trembling for the ark. Told that his sons are dead and the ark captured, he falls backward from his seat, breaks his neck, and dies.

l: Samuel, The First Book of Samuel
s: Samuel is a man whose life spans from birth to death and beyond, serving as prophet, judge, seer and kingmaker of Israel. Born to Hannah after the LORD remembered her, he was named because she asked him of the LORD, and was given to the LORD for all his life. As a child he served before Eli the priest at Shiloh in a linen ephod, grew in favor with the LORD and men, and heard the LORD call him, delivering a message of judgment against Eli's house. All Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew him as an established prophet whose words did not fall to the ground. He later exhorted Israel to put away foreign gods, gathered them at Mizpah, prayed and offered a lamb, and set up the Ebenezer stone. He judged Israel all his life on a yearly circuit of Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah, returning to his home at Ramah, where he built an altar. When old, he made his sons Joel and Abijah judges, but the elders asked for a king. Displeased, he prayed, warned the people of a king's ways, and, told by the LORD to comply, anointed Saul, first as prince and then as king, and wrote the regulations of the kingdom in a book. In his farewell he stated he was old and gray-headed, had walked before Israel from youth, and had taken nothing from anyone, which the people confirmed; he promised to keep praying and instructing them. His relationship with Saul then broke down: he rebuked Saul at Gilgal for offering the sacrifice before he arrived, then for sparing Amalek, declaring that obedience is better than sacrifice and that the kingdom was torn from Saul. He cut Agag in pieces, went to Ramah, and did not see Saul again before Saul's death, though he mourned him. Told to stop mourning, he went to Bethlehem and anointed David among his brothers. David later came to him at Ramah and they lived at Naioth, where Samuel stood as head of the company of the prophets. He died and was buried at his house in Ramah, mourned by all Israel. Even so, the woman at Endor brought him up, appearing as an old man in a robe, and he told Saul the LORD had become his adversary, had given the kingdom to David, and that Saul and his sons would join him the next day.

l: LORD, The First Book of Samuel
s: The LORD (also the LORD of Armies) is the God of Israel, presented as holy beyond compare, a rock, a God of knowledge, a living God, and the Strength of Israel who does not lie or repent. He sits above the cherubim, owns the pillars of the earth, judges its ends, and gives strength to his king. He is Israel's king, who delivered them out of Egypt and appointed Moses and Aaron. The records open at Shiloh, where he shuts and opens Hannah's womb and answers her vow with a son. Hannah's song praises him as one who kills and makes alive and raises the needy. He judges Eli's house, then calls Samuel and reveals himself to him by his word, letting none of Samuel's words fall. When the ark is taken, he strikes the Philistines and their god Dagon with tumors and panic, but also strikes the men of Beth Shemesh who looked into it, who call him a holy God. He answers Samuel, thunders against the Philistines, and opposes them all Samuel's days. When the people demand a human king, he tells Samuel they have rejected him, yet grants it and designates Saul as prince, anointing him and sending his Spirit. Saul's disobedience, especially regarding Amalek, leads the LORD to regret the choice and reject him as king. He then chooses David, looking at the heart rather than appearance, and his Spirit comes on David and departs from Saul, troubling Saul with an evil spirit. David trusts him as the living God who delivers from lion, bear and Goliath, since the battle is the LORD's. The LORD is with David, answers his inquiries, does not give him up to Saul, strikes Nabal, and puts Saul's camp into deep sleep. He is invoked as witness between David and Jonathan. Finally, he does not answer Saul, becomes his adversary, tears the kingdom from him and gives it to David, and he guides David to recover all from the raiders.

l: Hophni, The First Book of Samuel
s: is_a priest [to the LORD] Hophni, a son of Eli, was with the ark when it was brought to the camp. He was slain in the battle.

l: Phinehas, The First Book of Samuel
s: Phinehas, a priest and son of Eli, accompanied the ark to the camp, was slain in battle, and left a pregnant wife.

l: Shiloh, The First Book of Samuel
s: Shiloh is a place of worship housing the LORD's house, where Elkanah yearly sacrificed to the LORD of Armies and Eli's sons served as priests. Hannah prayed there and brought Samuel. Later the ark was taken from Shiloh to battle, defeat was announced to the city, and Eli died at its gate.

l: Ramah, The First Book of Samuel
s: Ramah is where David comes to Samuel after fleeing Saul, and where Naioth is located. Saul goes to Ramah, comes to the great well in Secu, asks where Samuel and David are, and is told they are at Naioth in Ramah.

l: Hannah's vow, The First Book of Samuel
s: promises Samuel [to give the boy to the LORD all his life, no razor on his head] Hannah vowed that if the LORD would look on her affliction and give her a boy, she would give him to the LORD all his life and no razor would touch his head. After Samuel's birth and weaning she fulfilled it by bringing him to Eli and declaring that she had given him to the LORD.

l: sons of Eli, The First Book of Samuel
s: Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are wicked men who did not know the LORD. They despise the LORD's offering, their servants seize raw meat by force, and they sleep with women serving at the Tent of Meeting, making their sin very great. They ignore their father's rebuke, and the LORD intends to kill them, with both dying in one day as the sign.

l: Israel, The First Book of Samuel
s: Israel is the people of the LORD, his chosen people, whose story in these records runs from defeat and repentance through the demand for a monarchy to the collapse of Saul's reign. It begins with defeats by the Philistines, about four thousand men lost and then thirty thousand, even after the ark is brought into camp. Israel then laments for twenty years, removes the Baals and Ashtaroth, serves the LORD only, fasts at Mizpah, and confesses sin. It pursues the Philistines, recovers its cities from Ekron to Gath, and has peace with the Amorites. The central turning point is the demand of the elders and people for a king like all the nations. The LORD notes Israel's long history of forsaking him since Egypt, and Samuel charges that the people rejected the LORD as their king. Saul is chosen, and Israel shouts 'Long live the king!', though some worthless fellows despise him. Israel comes out as one man at Bezek, three hundred thousand plus thirty thousand from Judah, wins the victory, and makes Saul king at Gilgal. After thunder and rain the people fear the LORD and confess adding this evil to their sins. They are told to keep following him and are warned that they and their king will be consumed if they keep doing evil. Under Saul, Israel's condition worsens. It is considered an abomination to the Philistines, hides in caves and scatters, and has no blacksmith, relying on the Philistines to sharpen farm tools, so only Saul and Jonathan have a sword or spear. The LORD saves Israel in battle, but the people sin by eating meat with blood and are distressed by Saul's oath. They refuse to let Jonathan die. The LORD rejects Saul and tears the kingdom of Israel from him. Israel flees when Goliath appears, then pursues the Philistines after David kills him, and all Israel loves David. After all Israel mourns Samuel, Saul encamps at Gilboa, and Samuel declares the army will be delivered to the Philistines. In the end the men of Israel flee and fall on Mount Gilboa. Saul and his sons die, and people beyond the valley and the Jordan abandon their cities, which the Philistines occupy.

l: sacrifice offerings (priests' custom), The First Book of Samuel
s: has_custom priest's servant takes meat with three-toothed fork [the priest takes all the fork brings up] The priests' custom was for a servant to stab a three-toothed fork into the pot and take whatever it brought up for the priest. The servant also demanded raw meat before the fat was burned, taking it by force if refused. This led the men to despise the LORD's offering.

l: house of your father, The First Book of Samuel
s: The house of the speaker's father, once in Egypt bondage, was chosen from all Israel's tribes as priests and given fire offerings. Despite a promise to walk before the LORD forever, a man of God announces it will be cut off, survivors begging for priestly posts for bread.

l: man of God, The First Book of Samuel
s: delivers_message_to Eli [prophecy of judgment on Eli's house] The man of God comes to Eli with the LORD's message of judgment. He recounts the house's privileges, accuses Eli of honoring his sons above the LORD, and announces the end of the house, the sign of the deaths of Hophni and Phinehas, and a coming faithful priest.

l: Hannah's song, The First Book of Samuel
s: is_spoken_by Hannah [prayer] Hannah's song exalts the LORD as holy, a rock, and a God of knowledge who weighs actions. It describes reversals in which the mighty are broken, the hungry are satisfied, the barren bears seven, and the poor are lifted from the dust. It ends by declaring that the LORD will judge the ends of the earth and strengthen his king and anointed.

l: house of Eli, The First Book of Samuel
s: Eli's house is a family under the LORD's declared judgment: he will fulfil everything spoken against it, forever, because Eli knew his sons brought a curse on themselves and did not restrain them; the iniquity, sworn, cannot be removed by sacrifice or offering.

l: Ark of the covenant, The First Book of Samuel
s: The ark of the covenant is the LORD's ark, belonging to the God of Israel. The elders bring it from Shiloh to the camp to save Israel, but the Philistines capture it in the second battle. They take it from Ebenezer to Ashdod, setting it beside Dagon, then to Gath and Ekron, where people are struck as it arrives. After seven months, the Philistine lords send it back on a new cart with golden jewels. At Beth Shemesh, men who looked into it die. It is then brought to Abinadab's house at Kiriath Jearim, where it stays twenty years.

l: vision, The First Book of Samuel
s: A rare vision, the LORD's message to Samuel announcing judgment on Eli's house; Samuel fears telling Eli, but when Eli demands it under a solemn charge, he reveals everything.

l: LORD's call to Samuel, The First Book of Samuel
s: The LORD calls Samuel three times; Samuel, not yet knowing the LORD, mistakes each for Eli's call. Eli then perceives it is the LORD and instructs him, and on the fourth call Samuel answers, 'Speak; for your servant hears.'

l: Philistines, The First Book of Samuel
s: The Philistines are a group of five-lord city-states (Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, Ekron) who worship Dagon and other gods, and who appear throughout these records as the persistent enemy of Israel and of King Saul. Their story is one of recurring war, with reversals in both directions, ending in a major victory over Saul. They first defeat Israel in two battles, killing four thousand and then thirty thousand, and capture the ark. Their gathering at Aphek precedes this. The ark, however, brings trouble: placed in Dagon's house at Ashdod and moved to Gath and Ekron, it leads their lords to consult priests and diviners. They return it with a trespass offering of five golden tumors and five golden mice, one per lord, and test whether the LORD's hand struck them by watching the cows go to Beth Shemesh. When they attack Israel at Mizpah, the LORD thunders and confuses them; they are routed, subdued, stop entering Israel's border, and the cities they took are restored. Later they regroup, encamp at Michmash with vast forces, send out raiders, and bar blacksmiths so the Hebrews cannot make swords or spears. Jonathan's attack throws their camp into panic, and they strike each other and flee. The war lasts all of Saul's days. At Socoh and Azekah they face Israel across a valley until their champion Goliath is killed; they flee, pursued to Gai and the gates of Ekron, and their camp is plundered. Saul hopes they will kill David, but David kills two hundred of them for the dowry. David also defeats them at Keilah, and a Philistine raid draws Saul away from pursuing David. The final movement begins with their armies gathering at Shunem and Aphek, with Achish drafting David before his dismissal. They terrify Saul, then fight Israel at Mount Gilboa, rout its men, and kill Saul's three sons. They cut off Saul's head, spread the news through their land, place his armor in the house of the Ashtaroth, fasten his body to the wall of Beth Shan, and occupy the cities Israelites abandoned.

l: Phinehas' wife, The First Book of Samuel
s: Eli's daughter-in-law, Phinehas' wife, hears the ark is taken and her husband and father-in-law dead, gives birth to Ichabod, ignores comforters, and dies.

l: Ichabod, The First Book of Samuel
s: named_meaning the glory has departed from Israel [explanation of the name given by his mother] Ichabod was born to Phinehas' wife as she was dying after the news of the ark's capture. His mother named him Ichabod, saying 'The glory has departed from Israel.'

l: man of Benjamin, The First Book of Samuel
s: is_from Benjamin [tribe] A man of Benjamin ran out of the army to Shiloh the same day, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. He told the city and then Eli that Israel had fled, Eli's sons were dead and the ark was captured.

l: battle between Israel and the Philistines, The First Book of Samuel
s: has_outcome Israel defeated [about 4,000 killed in first engagement; 30,000 footmen fell in second] Israel encamped beside Ebenezer and the Philistines at Aphek; in the first fight Israel lost about four thousand men. After the ark was brought, a second battle ended in a great slaughter of thirty thousand Israelite footmen, the ark's capture and the deaths of Hophni and Phinehas.

l: Dagon, The First Book of Samuel
s: Dagon is a Philistine god with a house in Ashdod. He is found fallen before the ark two mornings running; reset once, then his head and palms are cut off on the threshold, leaving his torso. Thereafter priests and visitors avoid stepping on that threshold.

l: Ashdod, The First Book of Samuel
s: Ashdod, a Philistine city, is where the ark is first brought; Dagon falls and breaks before it, and the LORD's hand strikes the city and borders with tumors.

l: people of Ashdod, The First Book of Samuel
s: has_state struck with tumors The people of Ashdod rise early to find Dagon fallen, and set him up again before finding him broken. They are struck with tumors, and the men conclude the ark of the God of Israel cannot stay with them. They gather the Philistine lords and have the ark carried to Gath.

l: Gath, The First Book of Samuel
s: has_state struck with tumors [men small and great] Gath receives the ark after Ashdod. The LORD's hand is against the city with a very great confusion, and men both small and great are struck so that tumors break out on them.

l: Ekron, The First Book of Samuel
s: has_state deadly panic [after ark arrived] Ekron receives the ark after it is sent from Gath. The city falls into deadly panic, the hand of God is very heavy there, and those who do not die are struck with tumors. The cry of the city goes up to heaven.

l: Ekronites, The First Book of Samuel
s: has_disposition fear of the ark [believed it would kill them] As the ark arrives, the Ekronites cry out that it has been brought to kill them and their people. They gather the Philistine lords and urge that the ark be sent away to its own place so it will not kill them.

l: tumors, The First Book of Samuel
s: is_a affliction [sent by the LORD on Philistine cities] Tumors are the affliction the LORD sends on Ashdod and its borders, then on the men of Gath, small and great. At Ekron, those who did not die were struck with them.

l: princes of the Philistines, The First Book of Samuel
s: distrust David [fear he would become an adversary in battle] The princes question the presence of the Hebrews and angrily insist that Achish send David back, fearing he would become an adversary in battle and reconcile himself to his lord with the heads of their men. They cite the song 'Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.' Their objection prevails and David is sent away.

l: trespass offering, The First Book of Samuel
s: A trespass offering to the LORD of five golden tumors and five golden mice, matching the Philistine lords' number and imaging the afflictions marring the land. It is placed in a box beside the ark on the cart, tumors assigned one each to five named cities.

l: new cart, The First Book of Samuel
s: has_property no yoke previously on its cows [cows had never been yoked] The new cart is prepared by the Philistines to carry the ark, with the box of golden jewels at its side. It is drawn by two cows to the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh and stops by a great stone. Its wood is then split for the burnt offering.

l: milk cows, The First Book of Samuel
s: Two never-yoked milk cows, calves shut up at home, are tied to a cart, head straight along the highway to Beth Shemesh lowing without turning, and are offered there as a burnt offering.

l: Beth Shemesh, The First Book of Samuel
s: has_part field of Joshua Beth Shemesh is the border town the cows head for, which the Philistines take as a sign that the LORD struck them. The ark comes to the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh, where a great stone remains to this day. The town suffers a great slaughter and then sends messengers to Kiriath Jearim.

l: people of Beth Shemesh, The First Book of Samuel
s: The people are reaping wheat in the valley when they see the ark and rejoice. They offer the cows as a burnt offering and make further sacrifices the same day. After the slaughter they mourn, ask who can stand before the holy God, and send messengers asking Kiriath Jearim to take the ark.

l: slaughter of Beth Shemesh men, The First Book of Samuel
s: The LORD strikes down fifty thousand seventy men of Beth Shemesh for looking into the ark; the people mourn, ask who can stand before the holy God, and send the ark to Kiriath Jearim.

l: Mizpah, The First Book of Samuel
s: is_place_of Samuel [he judged Israel there] Mizpah is where Israel gathers to fast, pour out water before the LORD, and confess their sin, and where Samuel judges them. Israel's men go out from Mizpah to pursue the Philistines, and Samuel sets the Ebenezer stone between Mizpah and Shen. It is one of the places on Samuel's yearly judging circuit.

l: Gilgal, The First Book of Samuel
s: Gilgal was where the people gathered after Saul and where Saul waited seven days for Samuel while the people scattered. There Saul offered the burnt offering and was rebuked by Samuel, who then left for Gibeah of Benjamin.

l: battle at Mizpah, The First Book of Samuel
s: has_outcome Philistines struck down [the LORD thundered and confused them] When the Philistines come near to fight Israel while Samuel is offering the burnt offering, the LORD thunders on them and confuses them, and they are struck down before Israel. Israel's men pursue them from Mizpah to under Beth Kar. Samuel marks the victory with a stone named Ebenezer, and the Philistines are subdued afterward.

l: sons (Samuel's sons), The First Book of Samuel
s: Samuel's sons Joel and Abijah, appointed judges over Israel at Beersheba, abandoned their father's ways, pursuing dishonest gain, taking bribes and perverting justice.

l: elders of Israel, The First Book of Samuel
s: request request for a king [to judge them like all the nations] The elders gathered and came to Samuel at Ramah. They cited his age and his sons' conduct as reasons and asked him to make them a king to judge them like all the nations.

l: people (Israel), The First Book of Samuel
s: Israel is a people brought out of Egypt by the LORD yet long inclined to forsake him for other gods. In Chapter 8, they refuse Samuel's warnings and demand a king to be like the nations, thereby rejecting the LORD as king.

l: king (requested by Israel), The First Book of Samuel
s: An unnamed king Israel demands to judge them and fight their battles like the nations' kings; despite warning that they will cry out unanswered, the LORD tells Samuel to give them one.

l: the way of the king, The First Book of Samuel
s: Samuel's warning describing the way of the king: he will take sons for chariots, horsemen, and labor, daughters as perfumers, cooks, and bakers, the best fields, vineyards, olive groves, a tenth of crops and flocks, and servants and donkeys. The people become his servants and cry out to the LORD in vain.

l: request for a king, The First Book of Samuel
s: Israel's demand for a king, made by the elders at Ramah citing Samuel's age and his sons' conduct, displeased Samuel and was called a rejection of the LORD as king. The LORD still told Samuel to grant it. Later, Samuel links it to Nahash's attack, calls it great wickedness, and the people confess it; the LORD will not forsake them.

l: Saul, The First Book of Samuel
s: Saul is a Benjamite, son of Kish, of the Matrite family, remembered as Israel's first king. He is introduced as a handsome young man, taller than all the people from the shoulders up, from the smallest tribe, sent to find lost donkeys. Through his servant he meets Samuel, who is told by the LORD that Saul is chosen. Anointed as prince over the LORD's inheritance, he receives another heart, prophesies among the prophets, hides among the baggage when chosen by lot at Mizpah, and is acclaimed king. Worthless fellows despise him, and he holds his peace. Coming in from the field behind his oxen, he is seized by God's Spirit, summons Israel by sending pieces of a yoke of oxen, defeats the Ammonites, shows mercy by refusing executions, and is made king at Gilgal. He reigns forty-two years, starting at thirty, fights enemies on every side including Moab, the Amalekites and above all the Philistines, and recruits valiant men. His family includes his wife Ahinoam, sons Jonathan, Ishvi and Malchishua, daughters Merab and Michal, and his captain Abner, who is also his uncle. The turning point comes when his fear leads him to offer the burnt offering himself instead of waiting for Samuel, and he is told his kingdom will not continue. His rash oath nearly costs Jonathan's life. After sparing Agag and the best livestock of Amalek, he is rejected as king by the LORD. The LORD's Spirit departs and an evil spirit torments him. He takes in David as armor bearer and loves him, but after David's victory over Goliath and the women's song he grows afraid and jealous. He hurls his spear, offers his daughters as snares, and hunts David with chosen men, even ordering the priests of Nob killed through Doeg. Twice David spares him, and Saul weeps, calls David more righteous, and acknowledges David will be king, yet the pursuit resumes until David flees to Gath. Abandoned by the LORD and afraid of the Philistine army, Saul consults the medium at Endor, though he had expelled mediums, and Samuel tells him that he and his sons will die. In the final battle at the Philistines' hands, he loses his sons, and when his armor bearer refuses to kill him, he falls on his own sword. The Philistines behead him and fasten his body to the wall of Beth Shan, until men of Jabesh Gilead retrieve and bury his bones.

l: Kish, The First Book of Samuel
s: Kish, a Benjamite mighty man of valor, son of Abiel and father of Saul, owns donkeys; when they are lost, he sends Saul and a servant to search.

l: servant (Saul's servant), The First Book of Samuel
s: owns silver (quarter shekel) [offered to the man of God] The servant accompanies Saul in the search and, at Zuph, proposes consulting the honored man of God in the city. He offers the fourth part of a shekel of silver as a gift when Saul worries they have nothing to bring. At the end Samuel has him go on ahead of Saul and Samuel.

l: donkeys (Kish's donkeys), The First Book of Samuel
s: has_state found [lost three days before] Kish's donkeys were lost, which prompted Saul's journey through Ephraim, Shalishah, Shaalim, and Benjamin, where they were not found. Samuel later tells Saul they were lost three days earlier and have been found.

l: city (where Samuel lives), The First Book of Samuel
s: located_in land of Zuph Saul and his servant go up to this city, where young maidens drawing water tell them the seer has just arrived for the people's sacrifice. Samuel meets them within it, and Saul talks with him on the housetop that night. They walk to the end of the city the next morning, where Samuel sends the servant ahead.

l: high place, The First Book of Samuel
s: The high place is where the people hold a sacrifice that day and where Samuel goes up to bless it before the invited guests eat. Samuel tells Saul to go up there ahead of him to eat. Afterward they come down from it into the city.

l: sacrifice feast, The First Book of Samuel
s: held_at high place The people hold a sacrifice at the high place, and they will not eat until Samuel arrives to bless it. Saul and his servant are seated in the best place among about thirty invited guests. Saul is served the reserved thigh that Samuel had told the cook to set aside for him.

l: band of prophets (near the hill of God), The First Book of Samuel
s: A band of prophets near the hill of God, playing lute, tambourine, pipe and harp, comes down from the high place prophesying as Samuel foretold; Saul meets them and prophesies among them.

l: kingdom of Israel, The First Book of Samuel
s: The kingdom begins as the people demand a king and Saul is chosen by lot at Mizpah and acclaimed. Samuel tells the people the regulations of the kingdom and writes them in a book laid up before the LORD. Saul is accompanied by an army whose hearts God had touched, though some despise him and bring no tribute.

l: Saul’s anointing, The First Book of Samuel
s: Samuel privately anoints Saul with oil, declaring him prince over the LORD's inheritance; confirming signs follow the same day, God gives Saul another heart, and Saul keeps it secret until Mizpah.

l: Nahash the Ammonite, The First Book of Samuel
s: Nahash, an Ammonite king of Ammon, besieges Jabesh Gilead and demands all its men's right eyes be gouged out for a covenant, to dishonor Israel, but Saul's army strikes and scatters his forces.

l: Jabesh Gilead, The First Book of Samuel
s: Jabesh Gilead is besieged by Nahash the Ammonite. Its elders obtain seven days to seek help, and the town is rescued by Saul and Israel the next day, as promised. Jabesh Gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, and its valiant men acted in response. The bodies of Saul and his sons were brought there, burned, and their bones buried under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh.

l: inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead, The First Book of Samuel
s: The inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead are a community whose elders, facing Nahash's demand to lose their right eyes, sent messengers across Israel, were promised rescue by the next day, and were delivered. Later, hearing of Saul's fate, their valiant men marched overnight, took the bodies from Beth Shan's wall, burned them, buried the bones under a tamarisk, and fasted seven days.

l: Ammonites, The First Book of Samuel
s: The Ammonites, under Nahash, are attacked by Saul's three companies in the morning watch and struck until the heat of the day. The survivors are scattered so that no two are left together.

l: rescue of Jabesh (battle against the Ammonites), The First Book of Samuel
s: The rescue of Jabesh Gilead: Israel musters at Bezek, messengers promise rescue by next day's heat; Saul splits the people into three companies, strikes the Ammonite camp at morning watch, and scatters them.

l: Saul's coronation at Gilgal, The First Book of Samuel
s: At Samuel's call to renew the kingdom, all the people gather at Gilgal, make Saul king before the LORD, offer peace offerings, and rejoice greatly.

l: thunder and rain, The First Book of Samuel
s: Thunder and rain sent by the LORD at Samuel's call during wheat harvest, meant to show the people their wickedness in asking for a king; it arrives that day and fills everyone with fear of the LORD and Samuel.

l: Jonathan, The First Book of Samuel
s: Jonathan is Saul's son and a warrior who leads one thousand men at Gibeah of Benjamin and strikes the Philistine garrison in Geba. He and Saul alone have a sword or spear on the day of battle. Acting in faith in the LORD's power to save, he secretly attacks another garrison with his young armor bearer, setting off a panic. Unaware of his father's oath, he eats honey, is chosen by lot, and Saul says he must die, but the people rescue him, crediting him with a great salvation in Israel and saying he worked with God. The story then turns to his bond with David. He loves David as his own soul, makes a covenant with him, and gives him his robe, sword, bow, and sash. He warns David of Saul's plans, defends him to Saul, and restores him to Saul's presence. After Saul rages and throws a spear at him, he accepts that David is doomed, grieves, carries out the arrow signal, and parts from David with an oath of peace. At the end he strengthens David's hand in God, affirms David will be king with Jonathan beside him, makes a covenant before the LORD, and returns home.

l: Michmash, The First Book of Samuel
s: Michmash was where two thousand of Saul's men were stationed at the start, and later where the Philistines encamped, east of Beth Aven. The Philistine garrison went out to the pass of Michmash.

l: burnt offering, The First Book of Samuel
s: Saul ordered the burnt offering and the peace offerings brought to him at Gilgal and offered the burnt offering himself. Samuel arrived as soon as he had finished.

l: Saul's disobedient offering (Saul's sacrifice at Gilgal), The First Book of Samuel
s: Saul's burnt offering at Gilgal was a violation of the LORD's commandment: after waiting seven days, with people scattering and Philistines gathering, he offered it without Samuel, who called it foolish and declared Saul's kingdom would not continue.

l: armor bearer (Jonathan's armor bearer), The First Book of Samuel
s: The armor bearer tells Jonathan to do all that is in his heart and says he is with him. He follows Jonathan up the crag and kills the Philistines who fall before Jonathan.

l: Saul's army (the people with Saul), The First Book of Samuel
s: has_size about six hundred men About six hundred men are with Saul and do not know Jonathan has gone. They come to the battle, keep the oath and grow faint, then pounce on the plunder and eat meat with blood, and bring their oxen and sheep to be killed properly. They refuse to let Saul put Jonathan to death and rescue him.

l: honey, The First Book of Samuel
s: effect_on_eater brightened eyes [Jonathan tasted it] Honey on the ground in the forest is left untouched by the people because of the oath. Jonathan dips his rod in it and eats, and his eyes brighten, which exposes his breaking of the oath and leads to the lot falling on him.

l: Saul's oath, The First Book of Samuel
s: Saul's oath is a curse forbidding anyone to eat before evening until he is avenged. It distresses the people, Jonathan unknowingly breaks it with honey and criticizes it, and the people prevent his punishment.

l: Amalekites, The First Book of Samuel
s: took_captive captives (families of David's men) [killed none] The Amalekites raid the South, Judah, Caleb's South, and Ziklag, burn Ziklag, and carry off the women and all who were in it without killing any. David's men find them spread over the ground eating, drinking, and dancing over the great plunder. David strikes them from twilight until the evening of the next day, and only four hundred young men on camels escape.

l: Michal, The First Book of Samuel
s: Michal is Saul's daughter who loves David. Saul, hoping she will snare David, gives her to him as wife after the dowry. She then saves David, warning him, lowering him through a window, and deceiving Saul's messengers with a teraphim in the bed. Saul later gives her to Palti.

l: Abner, The First Book of Samuel
s: Abner is captain of Saul's army and serves Saul. In Chapter 26 he sleeps beside Saul while David takes the spear and water jar, then David rebukes him from a distant mountain for failing to guard the king.

l: battle against the Philistines at Michmash, The First Book of Samuel
s: Battle at Michmash: Jonathan and his armor bearer kill about twenty Philistines, panic and an earthquake follow, Saul's people and turned Hebrews and hidden Israelites join, the Philistines flee to Aijalon, and the LORD saves Israel.

l: Amalek, The First Book of Samuel
s: opposes Israel [set himself against Israel on the way out of Egypt] Amalek is to be struck and utterly destroyed because of how it set itself against Israel on the way up out of Egypt. Saul strikes the Amalekites from Havilah to Shur and destroys all the people with the sword except King Agag, though the Kenites living among them are warned away and spared.

l: Agag, The First Book of Samuel
s: Agag, king of the Amalekites, is captured alive and spared by Saul with the best livestock. He approaches Samuel confident death has passed, but Samuel condemns him for making women childless and cuts him down at Gilgal.

l: people (Saul's army), The First Book of Samuel
s: has_size 210,000 [two hundred thousand footmen and ten thousand men of Judah] The people, Saul's army, join Saul in sparing Agag and the best of the livestock while destroying only what was vile and refuse. Saul blames them for taking the plunder to sacrifice at Gilgal, and later says he feared the people and obeyed their voice.

l: plunder (Amalekite livestock spared), The First Book of Samuel
s: is_intended_for sacrifice [to the LORD at Gilgal, per Saul] The best of the sheep, cattle, fat calves, lambs and all that was good are kept rather than destroyed, while only the worthless animals are destroyed. Samuel exposes it by the bleating and lowing he hears. Saul claims the animals were kept to sacrifice to the LORD at Gilgal, but Samuel calls taking the plunder evil in the LORD's sight.

l: Saul's disobedience and rejection as king, The First Book of Samuel
s: involves plunder (Amalekite livestock spared) [Saul and the people spared the best livestock instead of destroying it] Saul's failure to destroy everything as commanded is the LORD's grounds for rejecting him as king. Samuel calls rebellion like witchcraft and stubbornness like idolatry, and says that because Saul rejected the LORD's word, the LORD rejected him. Saul's confession and plea do not reverse it, and the torn robe symbolizes the kingdom being torn from him.

l: Jesse, The First Book of Samuel
s: Jesse is an elderly Ephrathite Bethlehemite whose youngest son is David. He presents seven sons to Samuel, none chosen by the LORD, then reveals David tending sheep, sends for him, and later sends him to Saul with bread, wine, and a goat.

l: David, The First Book of Samuel
s: David is a man introduced as Jesse's youngest son, a ruddy, handsome shepherd from Bethlehem, anointed among his brothers, after which the LORD's Spirit comes mightily on him. He is a skillful harp player and becomes Saul's armor bearer. Having killed a lion and a bear, he trusts the LORD and kills Goliath in the valley of Elah with a sling and stone, despite Eliab's anger and Saul's doubts. He then rises in Saul's service: he behaves wisely, becomes captain of a thousand, kills two hundred Philistines, and marries Michal, becoming Saul's son-in-law and highly esteemed. Jonathan says he will be king of Israel, and they make a covenant before the LORD. Saul's jealousy, sparked by the song that David has slain ten thousands, turns to pursuit. Saul's spear, messengers at his house, and daily searching force David to flee, aided by Michal, Samuel, Jonathan and Ahimelech. He gathers about four hundred men at Adullam, later six hundred, and habitually inquires of the LORD, saving Keilah from the Philistines yet leaving when told its men would betray him. In the wildernesses of Ziph and Maon and at En Gedi he twice spares Saul, cutting only a skirt of his robe and later taking his spear and water jar, because Saul is the LORD's anointed. He swears not to cut off Saul's offspring and relies on the LORD as judge. Saul acknowledges him as his anointed-king-to-be and calls him son. David turns back from vengeance on Nabal at Abigail's plea and marries her and Ahinoam of Jezreel. Fearing Saul, he goes to Achish at Gath and receives Ziklag, where he lives a year and four months, raiding Amalekites and others and deceiving Achish, who trusts him as an upright servant like an angel of God. The Philistine princes reject him as a Hebrew, and he departs. He finds Ziklag burned and his wives taken, and his men talk of stoning him, but he strengthens himself in the LORD, pursues the Amalekites, recovers everything, shares plunder equally among all his men, and sends gifts to the elders of Judah.

l: evil spirit, The First Book of Samuel
s: troubles Saul [sent from the LORD] An evil spirit from the LORD (called an evil spirit from God by Saul's servants) troubles Saul after the LORD's Spirit leaves him. It departs from him whenever David plays the harp, leaving Saul refreshed and well.

l: anointing of David, The First Book of Samuel
s: Samuel anoints David with oil from a horn in the middle of his brothers, after the LORD rejects the other seven sons and says, "Arise! Anoint him, for this is he." From that day forward the LORD's Spirit comes mightily on David.

l: Goliath the Philistine, The First Book of Samuel
s: Goliath of Gath is a towering Philistine champion, six cubits and a span tall, armed with bronze helmet, mail, shin armor, javelin, and an iron-headed spear, with a shield bearer. He challenges Israel for forty days to send a man to fight, the loser's side becoming servants, and curses David. David strikes his forehead with a stone, then beheads him with his own sword.

l: valley of Elah, The First Book of Samuel
s: The valley of Elah is where Saul and the men of Israel encamp and set the battle in array against the Philistines. The Philistines stand on one mountain and Israel on the other, with the valley between them, and it is where David kills Goliath.

l: sling and stone, The First Book of Samuel
s: David chooses five smooth stones from the brook, puts them in his shepherd's bag, and carries his sling in his hand. He slings one stone, which sinks into Goliath's forehead and fells him, so that David prevails with a sling and a stone without a sword in his hand.

l: sword of Goliath, The First Book of Samuel
s: Goliath the Philistine's sword, taken after David killed him in the valley of Elah, was kept wrapped in cloth behind the ephod at Nob; Ahimelech gave it to David, who called it unmatched and took it.

l: battle between David and Goliath, The First Book of Samuel
s: Goliath advances toward David with his shield bearer before him, curses David by his gods, and threatens to give his flesh to the birds and animals. David answers that he comes in the name of the LORD of Armies, runs toward the army to meet him, and fells him with one stone. David then stands over Goliath, draws Goliath's sword, and cuts off his head, causing the Philistines to flee.

l: covenant (between Jonathan and David), The First Book of Samuel
s: David appeals to the covenant of the LORD that Jonathan brought him into, and Jonathan renews it with David's house, asking that David show kindness to his house forever. At parting they again affirm that the LORD is between them and between their offspring forever.

l: dowry of one hundred Philistine foreskins, The First Book of Samuel
s: A bride-price Saul demands for Michal, claiming to avenge the king's enemies but secretly hoping the Philistines will kill David. David doubles it with two hundred foreskins, delivers them in full, and wins Michal.

l: David's four hundred men, The First Book of Samuel
s: About four hundred men in distress, debt, or discontent gather to David at Adullam's cave; he becomes their captain, and his brothers and father's house join him there.

l: messengers (Saul's messengers), The First Book of Samuel
s: Saul sends messengers to watch David's house and kill him in the morning, but Michal says he is sick and they find only the teraphim in the bed. Saul later sends three successive groups of messengers to seize David at Naioth, and each group is overcome by God's Spirit and prophesies instead.

l: company of the prophets, The First Book of Samuel
s: The company of the prophets is seen prophesying at Naioth with Samuel standing as head over them. Saul's messengers who come to seize David join in the prophesying when God's Spirit comes on them.

l: teraphim (Michal's decoy in David's bed), The First Book of Samuel
s: Michal lays the teraphim in David's bed, puts a pillow of goats' hair at its head, and covers it with clothes to make it look like a sick man. When Saul's messengers come in, they find the teraphim in the bed instead of David, exposing the deception.

l: Naioth in Ramah, The First Book of Samuel
s: located_in Ramah Naioth, in Ramah, is where David and Samuel go to live after David's escape. Saul is told David is there, and his messengers and then Saul himself are overcome by God's Spirit and prophesy there.

l: Saul's prophesying and nakedness, The First Book of Samuel
s: An episode in which Saul, going to Naioth, is seized by God's Spirit, prophesies, strips his clothes, and lies naked before Samuel all day and night, giving rise to the proverb "Is Saul also among the prophets?"

l: boy (Jonathan's boy), The First Book of Samuel
s: Jonathan's servant boy accompanies him to the field, runs to fetch shot arrows, remains ignorant of the secret arrow signal known only to Jonathan and David, and is finally sent back to the city carrying Jonathan's weapons.

l: arrows (Jonathan's arrows), The First Book of Samuel
s: Jonathan plans to shoot three arrows by the stone Ezel as a secret signal: arrows on this side of the boy mean peace, arrows beyond him mean David must go. Jonathan shoots an arrow beyond the boy and calls out that it is beyond him, confirming the danger to David.

l: new moon feast (Saul's table), The First Book of Samuel
s: The new moon feast is the occasion David says he should attend and the test of Saul's intentions. David's seat is empty on both days, which leads to Saul's questioning, his outburst against Jonathan, and the throwing of his spear, after which Jonathan leaves the table in fierce anger.

l: spear (Saul's spear), The First Book of Samuel
s: belongs_to Saul Saul's spear is stuck in the ground at his head as he sleeps, and Abishai wants to use it to strike him. David instead takes it away, shows it from the mountain as proof of how close he came, and offers to have a young man come over and retrieve it.

l: Ahimelech, The First Book of Samuel
s: Ahimelech, son of Ahitub, is a priest at Nob. He receives a trembling, solitary David, giving him holy bread and Goliath's sword. Saul later summons him, accusing him of conspiracy with David. Ahimelech defends himself, praising David's faithfulness and claiming ignorance of any plot, yet Saul sentences him and his father's whole house to death.

l: Nob, The First Book of Samuel
s: is_a city of the priests Nob is the city of the priests, where Ahimelech lived and where David had received food and Goliath's sword. Doeg struck it with the sword, killing men, women, children, nursing babies, and its cattle, donkeys, and sheep.

l: holy bread, The First Book of Samuel
s: Holy bread is show bread taken from before the LORD, eaten only by men who kept from women. Ahimelech, having no common bread, gave it to David after his assurance, as it was being replaced with hot bread.

l: Doeg the Edomite, The First Book of Samuel
s: Doeg, an Edomite and Saul's chief herdsman, informs Saul that David visited Ahimelech at Nob; when Saul's guards refuse, Doeg kills eighty-five priests and destroys Nob. David had foreseen his betrayal.

l: Achish, The First Book of Samuel
s: Achish, son of Maoch, is king of Gath and a Philistine leader. David first flees to him and feigns madness, so Achish rebukes his servants and refuses to admit him. Later he receives David and his men and gives him Ziklag, believing David's false report of raiding Judah means Israel abhors him and he will serve forever. Finally Achish defends David to the Philistine princes, finding no fault in him and calling him upright, but yields to them and sends David away in peace at first light.

l: David's feigned insanity, The First Book of Samuel
s: David, afraid after Achish's servants recognized him, feigns madness by scribbling on gate doors and drooling into his beard, convincing Achish he is insane and wants nothing to do with him.

l: Abiathar, The First Book of Samuel
s: Abiathar, priest and son of Ahimelech, sole survivor of the priests of Nob, escaped Saul's massacre, fled to David with the ephod, reported the killings, and received David's promise of safety.

l: priests of Nob, The First Book of Samuel
