s: Saul summoned Ahimelech and all his father's house, the priests at Nob, and condemned them for allegedly aiding David. The king's servants refused to raise a hand against these priests of the LORD, but Doeg killed eighty-five of them. Only Abiathar escaped.

l: massacre of Nob, The First Book of Samuel
s: Massacre at Nob: on Saul's order, Doeg the Edomite killed eighty-five priests and then the city's men, women, children, infants and livestock after Saul's servants refused; only Abiathar escaped to David, who accepted responsibility.

l: Keilah, The First Book of Samuel
s: Keilah is a walled town with gates and bars, raided by Philistines at its threshing floors; David saves it, but facing Saul's siege and its men's betrayal, he leaves.

l: David's men, The First Book of Samuel
s: David's men are a company of about six hundred who follow David through his years as a fugitive. They fear going to Keilah yet fight and save its people, then accompany him in the wilderness of Maon and into the cave's innermost parts, where they urge him to seize his enemy Saul, but he restrains them. They go with their households to Achish at Gath, settle in Ziklag, and raid neighboring peoples. Finding Ziklag burned and their families taken, they grieve and speak of stoning David. Four hundred pursue the Amalekites, recover everything, and David overrules those objecting to sharing the plunder.

l: Ziphites, The First Book of Samuel
s: The Ziphites are residents of the wilderness of Ziph who betray David by reporting his hiding place to Saul at Gibeah and offering to deliver him; Saul blesses them and sends them to confirm.

l: wilderness of Ziph, The First Book of Samuel
s: David stays in the strongholds and woods of the wilderness of Ziph while Saul seeks him daily. Jonathan visits him there and they make a covenant.

l: wilderness of Maon, The First Book of Samuel
s: is_located_in Arabah [south of the desert] David and his men move to the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah south of the desert, when Saul comes seeking him. Saul pursues him there and nearly surrounds him on the mountain until the Philistine raid calls Saul away, and the place is named Sela Hammahlekoth.

l: cave (near the sheep pens), The First Book of Samuel
s: is_located_near sheep pens [by the way] The cave by the sheep pens is where Saul goes in to relieve himself while David and his men stay in its innermost parts. It is the place where David cuts off Saul's skirt and spares his life. Saul leaves the cave and goes on his way, and David follows afterward.

l: skirt of Saul's robe, The First Book of Samuel
s: is_part_of Saul [part of his robe, cut off by David] David secretly cuts off the skirt of Saul's robe in the cave, and his heart strikes him afterward for doing so. He holds it up to Saul as proof that he had the chance to kill him and did not, showing there is neither evil nor disobedience in his hand.

l: Abigail, The First Book of Samuel
s: Abigail is an intelligent, beautiful woman, wife of Nabal the Carmelite, attended by five maids. She quickly sends food to David, bows, takes blame, and turns him from vengeance by speaking of his future. She tells Nabal in the morning; after his death she becomes David's wife.

l: Nabal, The First Book of Samuel
s: Nabal, a very wealthy man of the house of Caleb living in Maon with holdings in Carmel, owns three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. Surly, evil and called a worthless fool, husband of Abigail, he scorns David's request, feasts drunkenly, becomes stone-like on hearing the danger, and dies ten days later struck by the LORD.

l: David's young men, The First Book of Samuel
s: protected Nabal's shepherds and young men [like a wall by night and day] Ten of David's young men go to Carmel, deliver David's greeting and request to Nabal in his name, and wait, only to be insulted and sent back. A young man of Nabal's later testifies that they were very good to Nabal's shepherds, acting as a wall by night and day. Four hundred of David's men put on swords to follow him while two hundred stay with the baggage, and Abigail's gift is given to them.

l: Abigail's gift, The First Book of Samuel
s: consists_of loaves, wine, sheep, grain, raisins and figs [two hundred loaves, two containers of wine, five dressed sheep, five seahs of parched grain, one hundred clusters of raisins, two hundred cakes of figs] Abigail gathers two hundred loaves of bread, two containers of wine, five dressed sheep, five seahs of parched grain, one hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and sends them ahead on donkeys without telling Nabal. She asks that it be given to David's young men, and David receives it from her hand and tells her to go up in peace.

l: Nabal's death, The First Book of Samuel
s: is_caused_by LORD [about ten days after Abigail told him] After Nabal learns in the morning what Abigail did, his heart dies within him and he becomes as a stone. About ten days later the LORD strikes him and he dies. David, hearing of it, blesses the LORD for pleading his cause and keeping him from evil, and then sends to take Abigail as his wife.

l: Nabal's insult to David's messengers, The First Book of Samuel
s: Nabal answers David's servants by asking who David and the son of Jesse are, saying many servants break away from their masters, and refusing to give his bread, water, and meat to men of unknown origin. The messengers return and report this to David, who then orders his men to put on their swords. One of Nabal's young men also tells Abigail that Nabal insulted the messengers even though David's men had protected the shepherds.

l: Abishai the son of Zeruiah, The First Book of Samuel
s: is_brother_of Joab Abishai, brother of Joab, volunteers to go down into Saul's camp with David. He urges David to let him strike Saul with the spear in one stroke, but David forbids it.

l: Ziklag, The First Book of Samuel
s: Ziklag is a city that Achish gives David when he asks for a place in the country; it thereafter belongs to the kings of Judah. The Amalekites raid and burn it, David and his men find it in ruins on the third day, and after victory David returns and sends plunder to Judah's towns.

l: David's raid on the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites, The First Book of Samuel
s: David's raid strikes the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites on the way to Shur and Egypt. He leaves no man or woman alive and takes sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels, and clothing. He then returns to Achish, falsely claiming he raided Judah's South, the Jerahmeelites, and Kenites.

l: David's flight to the Philistines, The First Book of Samuel
s: David, deciding escape is best, flees with his six hundred men to Achish of Gath in Philistine country, hoping Saul will give up searching; Saul stops pursuing him, and David stays a year and four months.

l: plunder (David's raid), The First Book of Samuel
s: The Amalekites' plunder from the Philistines' land and Judah is recovered by David, with nothing lacking, small or great. David also takes the flocks and herds the Amalekites drove before their other livestock and calls them David's plunder. He shares it equally among all his men and sends part to the elders of Judah and many towns.

l: woman at Endor, The First Book of Samuel
s: A medium at Endor with a familiar spirit, she fears Saul's persecution of such practitioners but, after his oath, brings up Samuel and recognizes the disguised Saul. She then urges the collapsed king to eat, killing her fattened calf and baking unleavened bread for him and his servants.

l: Mount Gilboa, The First Book of Samuel
s: Mount Gilboa was the site where the men of Israel fell slain before the Philistines. Saul and his three sons died there, and the Philistines found their bodies there the next day when they came to strip the slain.

l: sons of Saul, The First Book of Samuel
s: Saul's sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua were killed by Philistines; their bodies, found on Mount Gilboa, were fastened to Beth Shan's wall, then taken by Jabesh Gilead's men, burned, and buried under a tamarisk tree.

l: Philistine-Israelite war, The First Book of Samuel
s: The Philistines gather and encamp at Shunem while Saul gathers Israel at Gilboa. Samuel foretells that Israel's army will be delivered into Philistine hands and that Saul and his sons will die the following day.

l: battle against Israel, The First Book of Samuel
s: The Philistines assemble at Aphek while the Israelites camp by the spring in Jezreel, setting the stage for battle. The princes refuse to let David go into it with them for fear he would turn against them. At the end of the unit the Philistines go up to Jezreel.

l: brook Besor, The First Book of Samuel
s: is_where two hundred faint men (left at Besor) [those left behind stayed there] The brook Besor is where David's six hundred men arrive and where those who are left behind stay. Two hundred men are too faint to cross it, so David continues with four hundred. David later meets the two hundred there on his return.

l: two hundred faint men (left at Besor), The First Book of Samuel
s: has_condition faint [could not cross the brook Besor] Two hundred of David's men are so faint that they cannot cross the brook Besor and stay behind. On David's return they come out to meet him and the people with him, and David greets them. Despite objections, David rules that they receive the same share of the plunder as those who fought.

l: Egyptian servant, The First Book of Samuel
s: A young Egyptian servant of an Amalekite was abandoned by his master when he fell sick. Found in a field and revived with food and water after three days, he describes the raid and Ziklag's burning, then, after David swears not to kill or return him, guides David to the Amalekite camp.

l: wicked men and worthless fellows, The First Book of Samuel
s: is_part_of David's men (David's army) [those who went with David] Among those who went with David, these men say the two hundred who did not go will receive none of the plunder, only their wives and children to lead away. David rebukes them, calling them brothers, and rejects their proposal.

l: captives (families of David's men), The First Book of Samuel
s: The wives, sons, and daughters of David's men, including David's wives Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite, are carried off alive by the Amalekites. David rescues them all, and none is lacking, whether small or great.

l: Amalekite raid on Ziklag, The First Book of Samuel
s: Amalekites raid the South and Ziklag while David and his men are away, burning Ziklag and capturing its people; the men's grief and anger lead David to pursue and defeat them.

l: statute of equal sharing, The First Book of Samuel
s: A statute established by David in Chapter 30 that plunder be shared equally between those who go down to battle and those who stay with the baggage; he made it an ordinance for Israel, still in force.

l: armor bearer (Saul's armor bearer), The First Book of Samuel
s: dies_by suicide [fell on his sword after Saul died] Saul's armor bearer refused to kill Saul because he was terrified. When he saw that Saul was dead after falling on his own sword, he likewise fell on his sword and died with him.

l: Beth Shan, The First Book of Samuel
s: has_part wall [Saul's body was fastened to it] The Philistines fastened Saul's body to the wall of Beth Shan. The bodies of his sons were also on that wall until the valiant men of Jabesh Gilead took them down.

l: Battle of Mount Gilboa, The First Book of Samuel
s: The Battle of Mount Gilboa pitted the Philistines against Israel, whose men fled and were slain. Saul's three sons died, Saul was wounded by archers and killed himself, and his armor bearer and men perished; Israelites then abandoned their cities.

l: Saul's death, The First Book of Samuel
s: occurs_at Mount Gilboa Saul, badly pressed by archers, asked his armor bearer to thrust him through so the uncircumcised could not abuse him. The armor bearer refused, so Saul fell on his own sword and died, and the armor bearer followed him in death. The Philistines then beheaded and stripped his body and fastened it to the wall of Beth Shan, and men of Jabesh Gilead later burned it and buried the bones.

l: The Second Book of Samuel
s: This is the Second Book of Samuel, a narrative of David's reign, following him from grief over Saul's death to the end of his rule. David is central; Joab, Abner, Absalom, Nathan, Michal, Mephibosheth, and Bathsheba matter most. After an Amalekite claims to have killed Saul, David mourns Saul and Jonathan, has the man executed, and composes a lament. David is anointed king of Judah at Hebron while Abner makes Ishbosheth king over the rest of Israel. War between the houses follows, with Asahel killed by Abner. Abner defects to David, Joab murders him, and David disowns the act. Ishbosheth is then killed by Baanah and Rechab, whom David punishes. All Israel anoints David, who takes Zion, defeats the Philistines, and brings the ark to Jerusalem after Uzzah's death; Michal despises his dancing. The LORD promises through Nathan an enduring house for David, whose victories widen and who shows kindness to Jonathan's son Mephibosheth. The narrative then turns: David sees Bathsheba, lies with her, and arranges the death of her husband Uriah. Nathan's parable confronts him, he confesses, their child dies, and Solomon is born. Family disaster follows: Amnon rapes Tamar, Absalom kills Amnon and flees, is brought back through Joab and the woman of Tekoa, then wins Israel's hearts and rebels. David flees Jerusalem; Ahithophel's counsel is defeated by Hushai, and Ahithophel hangs himself. Joab kills Absalom against David's command, David's grief nearly costs him the people, and he returns to power. Sheba's revolt is ended, with Joab killing Amasa. The closing chapters include a famine tied to Saul's killing of the Gibeonites and the hanging of seven of Saul's sons, wars with Philistine giants, David's song of deliverance, his last words, and a list of his mighty men. Finally David orders a census, confesses his sin, chooses pestilence that kills seventy thousand, and buys Araunah's threshing floor, builds an altar, and the plague stops.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel
s: David is a king, chosen by the LORD from the sheep pen to be prince over Israel, son of Jesse, and called the LORD's servant, anointed, and sweet psalmist. The records follow him from Ziklag, where he mourns Saul and Jonathan and has the Amalekite messenger executed for killing the LORD's anointed. He then goes to Hebron, where the men of Judah anoint him king and he reigns seven years and six months. There he has wives including Ahinoam, Abigail and Eglah, and six sons, among them Amnon, Chileab and Absalom. He regains Michal through Abner's alliance, declares himself innocent of Abner's murder, and admits he is weak against Zeruiah's sons. He also punishes Ishbosheth's killers. The elders anoint him over all Israel, and he reigns forty years in all, thirty-three of them in Jerusalem. He takes Zion, makes it David's city, defeats the Philistines, and brings the ark in with dancing and sacrifice. The LORD promises him an everlasting house and throne, and he answers in humble prayer. He subdues Philistines, Moab, Syria and Edom, rules with justice and righteousness, and keeps an administration headed by Joab, Zadok, Benaiah and others. He shows kindness to Mephibosheth for Jonathan's sake and later spares him because of their oath. The middle of the records turns to failure and family strife. He takes Bathsheba, arranges Uriah's death, and confesses 'I have sinned' when Nathan confronts him. Solomon is born. Amnon's rape of Tamar and Absalom's revolt follow, and David flees Jerusalem, weeps, endures Shimei's curses, and crosses the Jordan to Mahanaim. He grieves deeply for Absalom, is rebuked by Joab, and returns, then puts his ten concubines in widowhood. Sheba's revolt is ended by Joab. Famine, the Gibeonites, and the burial of Saul's bones follow, and his men insist he stop going to battle. The close shows him delivered by the LORD in song, speaking last words about an everlasting covenant, pouring out water won at risk by his mighty men, and numbering the people against Joab's objection. He confesses sin, pleads that the LORD's hand fall on him and his father's house, buys Araunah's threshing floor, refuses sacrifices that cost him nothing, and builds an altar.

l: Saul, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Saul, son of Kish and father of Jonathan, is remembered as the LORD's anointed and chosen one. David laments him as lovely, pleasant, swifter than eagles and stronger than lions, whose sword never returned empty. He clothed the daughters of Israel in scarlet and gold, and had a concubine, Rizpah. He died on Mount Gilboa, killed at his own request by an Amalekite, who took his crown and bracelet. Later, his land passes to his grandson Mephibosheth, with Ziba as his servant. Saul is blamed for a famine after killing the Gibeonites despite Israel's oath; seven descendants are hanged in atonement. His bones and Jonathan's are finally buried in Zela in Kish's tomb.

l: Jonathan, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Jonathan is a son of Saul, described as lovely and pleasant, whom David calls brother and whose love surpassed the love of women. He owns a bow that never turned back from the blood of the slain. He is reported dead with Saul, and David mourns him in a lamentation. His memory drives David's kindness toward his lame son Mephibosheth. Later, a Jonathan stays at En Rogel with Ahimaaz as David's messenger, evades being seen, hides in a well at Bahurim, and urges David to cross the water quickly.

l: Amalekite young man (the man who told David of Saul's death), The Second Book of Samuel
s: An Amalekite, son of a foreigner, arrives at David's camp from Saul's with torn clothes and earth on his head. He reports Saul's and Jonathan's deaths, claims he killed Saul at Saul's request, and brings the crown and bracelet. David has him executed for slaying the LORD's anointed.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Israel is the people of the LORD, a nation redeemed from Egypt and established as God's people forever, and also the land or place the LORD promises to appoint for them so they dwell there, no longer moved or afflicted. Across the records it appears mainly as a collective of tribes, their elders and men, whose loyalty to David shifts repeatedly. The account opens with mourning: Israel's people flee battle, many fall, and the lament calls Israel's glory slain and bids the daughters of Israel weep over Saul. All the tribes then come to David at Hebron, call themselves his bone and flesh, make a covenant, and anoint him king. Thirty thousand chosen men and the whole house of Israel celebrate bringing up the ark, and David is appointed prince over Israel. The LORD promises Israel a place, and David's prayer affirms its unique status. Israel's forces defeat the Syrians twice, and kings serving Hadadezer make peace and serve them. Division follows: Absalom steals the hearts of Israel's men, they cross the Jordan with him, and Israel is struck down in the forest of Ephraim, twenty thousand slain, before all flee to their tents. The people then debate bringing David back, and the men of Israel quarrel with Judah, claiming ten parts in the king. Some then follow Sheba, who dies, and the people disperse. The close shows Israel under the LORD's anger, counted from Dan to Beersheba with 800,000 swordsmen, and seventy thousand die in a pestilence that is removed after David's offerings.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Judah is a group of men loyal to David. They anoint him king at Hebron over the house of Judah while Ishbosheth reigns over Israel, and later unite as one to bring him back over the Jordan, answering Israel's complaints fiercely.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Samuel
s: The LORD, also called the God of Armies, is the God of Israel, presented as unique, with no other god or rock besides him, whose words are truth and whose way is perfect. He redeemed Israel out of Egypt and established Israel as his people forever. He has not lived in a house since then, moving about in a tent and tabernacle, and he sits above the cherubim. Most of the records concern his relationship with David, whom he established as king over Israel, having sworn to move the kingdom from Saul's house. He is David's rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, and lamp, and he executes vengeance on David's enemies. The account unfolds in stages. In Chapter 5 he is with David, makes him grow greater, and answers David's inquiries about the Philistines, going out before him in battle. In Chapter 6 his anger burns against Uzzah, whom he strikes dead beside the ark, while he blesses Obed-Edom's house. In Chapter 7 he refuses the idea of a cedar house and promises David a great name, rest for Israel, and an offspring whose throne he will establish forever, as a father who chastens but does not withdraw loving kindness. Chapter 11 notes that David's deed displeased him. In Chapter 12 he judges David through Nathan, puts away David's sin so he will not die, strikes the child with sickness, and loves Solomon. In Chapter 21 he answers David's seeking, declaring the famine is due to Saul's killing of the Gibeonites, and then answers prayer for the land after the bones are buried. Chapter 22 is a song praising his rescue, righteous rewards, and deliverance of the afflicted. Chapter 23 calls him the God and Rock of Israel, who made an everlasting covenant with David's house and worked great victories. In Chapter 24 he is angry with Israel, moves David to take a census, sends a pestilence that kills seventy thousand, then relents and is entreated for the land after David's sacrifices.

l: Philistines, The Second Book of Samuel
s: The Philistines are a group recurrently at war with Israel and opposed to David. They had hanged the bodies of Saul and Jonathan at Beth Shan. After David's anointing they go up to seek him, spreading themselves in the valley of Rephaim, where he strikes them at Baal Perazim and later from Geba to Gezer. David subdues them, takes the bridle of the mother city, and dedicates their silver and gold to the LORD. Their giants, descended from the giant of Gath, are killed, and warriors like Eleazar and Shammah defeat them, even as their garrison holds Bethlehem.

l: battle on Mount Gilboa, The Second Book of Samuel
s: A battle on Mount Gilboa, known through the Amalekite's report: Israel's people fled and many fell, Saul and Jonathan died, Saul pursued by chariots and horsemen. David then laments, wishing Gilboa no dew or rain, since the mighty's shield was defiled.

l: song of the bow (David's lamentation), The Second Book of Samuel
s: A lamentation by David over Saul and Jonathan, written in the book of Jashar and commanded to be taught to Judah's children. It opens with the refrain "How the mighty have fallen," asks that the news be kept from Gath and Ashkelon, praises both, urges Israel's daughters to weep for Saul, and closes mourning Jonathan.

l: Hebron, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Hebron is a city David is directed by the LORD to go up to, where his men and their households settle. Judah anoints him king there, and he reigns over Judah seven years and six months. Events there include the birth of his six sons, Abner's feast and killing at the gate, and Abner's burial with David weeping. Israel's tribes and elders later covenant with David and anoint him king. Finally, Absalom uses Hebron as a pretext for a vow and as the base for proclaiming himself king.

l: David's servants, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Envoys serving David, sent to comfort Hanun among the Ammonites, were humiliated with half-shaved beards and cut garments; David told them to wait at Jericho until regrowth.

l: Abner, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Abner, son of Ner, is captain of Saul's army who installs Ishbosheth as king over Gilead, Ephraim, Benjamin and all Israel. He proposes the contest at Gibeon, loses the battle, and kills Asahel after repeated warnings, then appeals to Joab to end the pursuit. Rebuked by Ishbosheth over Rizpah, he vows to transfer the kingdom to David and persuades Israel's elders. After feasting with David in Hebron, Joab kills him; David mourns him as a prince and great man.

l: Ishbosheth, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Ishbosheth, a son of Saul, was made king over Israel by Abner at Mahanaim at age forty and reigned two years. He feared Abner and could not answer his furious reply about Rizpah, and he complied with David's demand to take Michal from Paltiel. After hearing Abner was dead, he grew feeble-handed. His captains Rechab and Baanah killed and beheaded him on his bed at midday, and his head was buried in Abner's grave in Hebron.

l: Joab, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Joab is a man, son of Zeruiah and brother of Asahel and Abishai, who serves King David as captain and commander of the army, leading David's servants, the mighty men, and eventually all the army of Israel. He carries a sword on a sash and has followers of his own. The records show him as a capable, ruthless, and sometimes defiant commander. His story begins at the pool of Gibeon, where he leads David's servants against Abner's party. After Asahel is killed by Abner, Joab and Abishai pursue Abner, but Joab blows the trumpet to stop the fighting when Abner appeals to him. He buries Asahel and travels all night to Hebron. Later he deceives Abner into returning and strikes him dead in the gate to avenge Asahel, and David curses his house. Sent by David, he defeats the Syrians, then leads the army against the Ammonites. He follows David's letter by placing Uriah where valiant men are, sends word of Uriah's death, and captures Rabbah, the royal city, urging David to come take it so that Joab's name is not given to it. He arranges for the woman of Tekoa to move the king, and brings Absalom back from Geshur. After Absalom has his barley field burned, Joab carries Absalom's plea to the king. In the rebellion, he leads a third of the army and thrusts three darts into Absalom's heart despite the king's command, then stops the pursuit and manages who carries the news. He confronts David over his weeping, after which David says he will make Amasa captain in his place. Joab then kills Amasa with a sword while greeting him as a brother, leads the pursuit of Sheba, besieges Abel of Beth Maacah, ends the siege when the wise woman offers Sheba's head, and is named over all the army of Israel. Finally, he objects to David's census but is overruled, leads the count, and reports 800,000 valiant men in Israel and 500,000 in Judah.

l: Abishai, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Abishai is a son of Zeruiah and brother of Joab, a warrior serving David. He is first given command of the rest of the people against the Ammonites, who flee before him. He then rescues the faint David by killing the Philistine Ishbibenob, after which David's men forbid David to fight alongside them. He is finally honored as captain of the three mighty men, having killed three hundred with his spear, though not counted among the three.

l: Asahel, The Second Book of Samuel
s: Asahel, son of Zeruiah, brother of Joab and member of the thirty, was swift as a wild gazelle. He relentlessly pursued Abner, ignored warnings, was killed by Abner's spear, and was buried in his father's Bethlehem tomb.

l: contest at the pool of Gibeon, The Second Book of Samuel
s: A contest at the pool of Gibeon, proposed by Abner, pitted twelve young men for Benjamin and Ishbosheth against twelve of David's servants. Each seized his opponent and stabbed him, so all fell together, naming the place Helkath Hazzurim. A very severe battle followed, in which David's servants beat Abner and Israel.
